'''Kate S. Carroll''' (born 1974) is an American chemist and professor of chemistry and biochemistry at [[Florida Atlantic University]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Kate S. Carroll – Department of Chemistry & Biochemistry |url=https://chemistry.fau.edu/directory/kate-carroll.php |publisher=Florida Atlantic University |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref> She pioneered in-cell chemoproteomic methods to map redox-sensitive cysteines and developed probes that capture distinct oxidation states.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paulsen |first1=C. E. |last2=Carroll |first2=K. S. |title=Peroxide-dependent sulfenylation of the EGFR catalytic site enhances kinase activity |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |year=2012 |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=57–64 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.748}}</ref> These advances transformed redox proteomics into a site-resolved, quantitative discipline and created new strategies for targeting oxidized proteins in disease.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fu |first1=L. |last2=Jung |first2=Y. |last3=Tian |first3=C. |last4=Ferreon |first4=J. C. |last5=Chen |first5=J. |last6=Carroll |first6=K. S. |title=Nucleophilic covalent ligand discovery for the cysteine redoxome |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |year=2023 |volume=19 |issue=11 |pages=1309–1319 |doi=10.1038/s41589-023-01371-2}}</ref>

==Early life and career==
Carroll grew up in Morgan Hill, California, a small agricultural community in southern Santa Clara County.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Morgan Hill Historical Context |url=https://www.morganhill.ca.gov/ |publisher=City of Morgan Hill |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref> At the time, the town was surrounded by orchards and was only beginning to feel the influence of Silicon Valley.

She studied biochemistry at [[Mills College]] in Oakland, earning her B.A. in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alumnae Spotlight: Kate S. Carroll |url=https://alumnae.mills.edu |publisher=Mills College |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref> She began graduate training at [[Stanford University]] with Dan Herschlag, where she worked on enzymatic catalysis and RNA biochemistry, before moving to the laboratory of Suzanne Pfeffer. She completed her Ph.D. in 2003, investigating the molecular mechanisms of receptor trafficking and the regulation of Rab GTPases in the secretory pathway.<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Carroll |first=Kate S. |title=Regulation of Rab GTPases in receptor trafficking |publisher=Stanford University |year=2003}}</ref>

From 2003 to 2006 she was a Damon-Runyon postdoctoral fellow at the University of California, Berkeley, working with Nobel laureate Carolyn Bertozzi.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bertozzi Group Alumni |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/bertozzi |publisher=UC Berkeley |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref> In Bertozzi's lab she focused on reductive sulfur metabolism in mycobacteria, an experience that introduced her to the chemical biology of cysteine and redox processes and shaped the trajectory of her later research.

In 2006 Carroll joined the faculty at the [[University of Michigan]] as an assistant professor of chemistry and a member of the Life Sciences Institute.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kate Carroll, U-M Life Sciences Institute |url=https://lsa.umich.edu/ |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref> Four years later she moved to [[The Scripps Research Institute]] in Jupiter, Florida, where she was appointed associate professor and later to full professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carroll Lab – The Scripps Research Institute |url=https://www.scripps.edu/carrolllab/ |publisher=Scripps Research |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref> In 2024 she accepted a faculty position as professor of chemistry and biochemistry at [[Florida Atlantic University]], continuing her work on chemical biology and redox proteomics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Kate S. Carroll – Department of Chemistry & Biochemistry |url=https://www.fau.edu/artsandletters/chemistry/people/faculty/carroll-kate.php |publisher=Florida Atlantic University |access-date=2025-09-25}}</ref>

==Research==
Carroll's research examines the chemistry and biology of protein cysteines and how their reversible oxidation regulates cellular function. Her group developed in-cell mapping methods that revealed redox-sensitive cysteines acting as molecular sensors in signaling, metabolism, and stress.<ref name="ChemRev2013">{{Cite journal |last1=Paulsen |first1=C. E. |last2=Carroll |first2=K. S. |title=Cysteine-mediated redox signaling: chemistry, biology, and tools for discovery |journal=Chemical Reviews |year=2013 |volume=113 |issue=7 |pages=4633–4679 |doi=10.1021/cr300163e}}</ref> She also designed chemoselective probes to detect specific oxidative modifications, enabling proteome-wide analysis and expanding opportunities for redox-based therapeutics.<ref name="AccChemRes2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Y. |last2=Carroll |first2=K. S. |title=Activity-Based Sensing for Site-Specific Proteomic Analysis |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |year=2019 |volume=52 |issue=1 |pages=20–31 |doi=10.1021/acs.accounts.9b00562}}</ref> Together, these approaches established site-specific cysteine oxidation as a central principle of redox biology.

Earlier studies of cysteine oxidation were confined to lysates, where modifications were unstable and prone to artifacts. Carroll's group overcame these barriers by capturing oxidation directly in living systems. Using these methods, they showed that oxidation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) functions as a reversible switch that enhances kinase activity<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Paulsen |first1=Candice E. |last2=Truong |first2=Thu H. |last3=Garcia |first3=Francisco J. |last4=Homann |first4=Arne |last5=Gupta |first5=Vinayak |last6=Leonard |first6=Stephen E. |last7=Carroll |first7=Kate Her group also developed probes for metastable oxidative states that evade conventional detection. Dimedone-based reagents such as DAz-2<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leonard |first1=Stephen E. |last2=Reddie |first2=Khalilah G. |last3=Carroll |first3=Kate S. |title=Mining the thiol proteome for |first1=Ling |last2=Liu |first2=Keke |last3=Ferreira |first3=Renan B. |last4=Carroll |first4=Kate S. |last5=Yang |first5=Jing |title=Proteome-Wide Analysis of Cysteine S-Sulfenylation Using a |first4=Kate S. |title=Wittig reagents for chemoselective sulfenic acid ligation and detection in proteins |journal=Nature Chemistry |year=2021 |volume=13 |issue=11 |pages=1140–1150 |doi=10.1038/s41557-021-00786-8 |pmid=34650238}}</ref> and aryl nitroso<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lo Conte |first1=Mauro |last2=Lin |first2=Jiusheng |last3=Wilson |first3=Mark A. |last4=Carroll |pmid=26039147 |pmc=4605140}}</ref> and diazene electrophiles (DiaAlk) provided tractable chemistry for sulfinic acids (–SO₂H).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Akter |first1=Shahriar |last2=Fu |first2=Long |last3=Jung |first3=Youngeun |last4=Conte |first4=Matthew L. |last5=Lawson |first5=John R. |last6=Lowther |first6=William T. |last7=Sun |first7=Ren |last8=Liu |first8=Keke |last9=Yang |first9=Jing |last10=Carroll |first10=Kate S. |title=Chemical proteomics reveals new targets of cysteine sulfinic acid reductase |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |year=2018 |volume=14 |issue=11 |pages=995–1004 |doi=10.1038/s41589-018-0116-2 |pmid=30297807}}</ref> These tools revealed oxidized cysteines across thousands of proteins, broadening the scope of redox biology and establishing new chemical strategies to interrogate oxidative modifications.  

Carroll's laboratory advanced quantitative redox proteomics by introducing the concepts of occupancy, exposure, and flux to distinguish static from dynamic oxidation. Using isotopically labeled WYneN paired with iodoacetamide, her team built dual-probe workflows that measured sulfenylated sites at partial occupancies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Yunlong |last2=Fu |first2=Ling |last3=Yang |first3=Jing |last4=Carroll |first4=Kate S. |title=Wittig reagents for chemoselective sulfenic acid ligation enable global site stoichiometry analysis and redox-controlled mitochondrial targeting |journal=Nature Chemistry |year=2021 |volume=13 |pages=1140–1150 |doi=10.1038/s41557-021-00767-2 |pmid=34650238}}</ref> These studies showed that low-occupancy events often act as molecular switches, while high-occupancy oxidation reshapes protein function more broadly. They also revealed kinetic hierarchies influenced by local environments and by sulfiredoxin, which repairs sulfinic acids and links redox control to immune signaling and tissue protection.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Akter |first1=Shahriar |last2=Fu |first2=Long |last3=Jung |first3=Youngeun |last4=Conte |first4=Matthew L. |last5=Lawson |first5=John R. |last6=Lowther |first6=William T. |last7=Sun |first7=Ren |last8=Liu |first8=Keke |last9=Yang |first9=Jing |last10=Carroll |first10=Kate S. |title=Chemical proteomics reveals targets of cysteine sulfinic acid reduction by sulfiredoxin |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |year=2018 |volume=14 |issue=11 |pages=995–1004 |doi=10.1038/s41589-018-0116-2 |pmid=30297807}}</ref>

Her research also highlighted the therapeutic potential of oxidized cysteines. EGFR oxidation was shown to enhance kinase activity, illustrating how oxidation can alter druggable states and affect covalent inhibitors.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Truong |first1=Thu H. |last2=Ung |first2=Peter Man Un |last3=Palde |first3=Prakash B. |last4=Paulsen |first4=Candice E. |last5=Schlessinger |first5=Avner |last6=Carroll |first6=Kate S. |title=Molecular Basis for Redox Activation of Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Kinase |journal=Cell Chemical Biology |year=2016 |volume=23 |issue=7 |pages=837–848 |doi=10.1016/j.chembiol.2016.05.017 |pmid=27320908}}</ref> Her group introduced a nucleophilic covalent ligand strategy that selectively targeted sulfenic acids, uncovering hundreds of previously inaccessible ligandable sites across the proteome.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fu |first1=Ling |last2=Jung |first2=Youngeun |last3=Tian |first3=Caiping |last4=Ferreira |first4=Renan B. |last5=Cheng |first5=Ruifeng |last6=He |first6=Fuchu |last7=Yang |first7=Jing |last8=Carroll They also devised a redox-triggered approach for mitochondrial targeting<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Yunlong |last2=Fu |first2=Ling |last3=Yang |first3=Jing |last4=Carroll |first4=Kate S. |title=Wittig reagents for chemoselective sulfenic acid ligation enable global site stoichiometry analysis and redox-controlled mitochondrial targeting |journal=Nature Chemistry |year=2021 |volume=13 |pages=1140–1150 |doi=10.1038/s41557-021-00767-2}}</ref> and showed that viral proteins, including the SARS-CoV-2 spike, depend on redox-sensitive cysteines for infection.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shi |first1=Yunlong |last2=Zeida |first2=Ari |last3=Edwards |first3=Caitlin E. |last4=Mallory |first4=Michael L. |last5=Sastre |first5=Santiago |last6=Machado |first6=Matías R. |last7=Pickles == Awards and honors ==
Carroll has received recognition for her contributions to chemical biology and redox proteomics. In 2013 she was awarded the [[American Chemical Society]] [[Pfizer Award in Enzyme Chemistry|Pfizer Award in Enzyme Chemistry]], one of the field's early-career honors presented annually to a scientist under 40 for distinguished contributions to understanding enzyme mechanisms and function. She was cited for developing [[Chemoproteomics|chemoproteomic]] methods to probe [[Cysteine|cysteine]] oxidation in living cells and for revealing how redox modifications regulate signaling pathways and protein activity. In her award lecture, Carroll emphasized the potential of these approaches to connect fundamental chemistry with biological regulation and to identify new opportunities for therapeutic intervention. She has also delivered invited lectures at national and international meetings, where her work has been noted for bridging enzymology, proteomics, and redox biology. She also was recognized for her commitment to education, receiving the Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Award in 2010<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dr. Kate S. Carroll - Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry : Florida Atlantic University - Charles E. Schmidt College of Science |url=https://chemistry.fau.edu/directory/kate-carroll.php |access-date=2026-04-27 |website=chemistry.fau.edu |language=en}}</ref> for her demonstration in leadership and innovation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Camille Dreyfus Teacher Scholar |url=https://www.dreyfus.org/camille-dreyfus-teacher-scholar/ |access-date=2026-04-27 |website=Dreyfus Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Professional service==
Carroll is an associate editor of ''[[Free Radical Biology & Medicine]]'' and previously held the same role at ''[[Chemical Research in Toxicology]]''. She has also served as a reviewer for the U.S. National Institutes of Health and National Science Foundation, including as a permanent member of the NIH Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A (SBCA) study section. She has served on the editorial boards of journals including ''[[Cell Chemical Biology]]'', ''Current Opinion in Chemical Biology'', ''[https://home.liebertpub.com/publications/antioxidants-and-redox-signaling/4 Antioxidants & Redox Signaling]'', ''[https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/redox-biochemistry-and-chemistry Redox Biochemistry and Chemistry]'', and the ''[[Journal of Biological Chemistry]]''. She was elected vice chair (2018) and chair (2020, 2022) of the Gordon Research Conference on [[Gordon Research Conferences|Thiol-Based Redox Regulation and Signaling]]. In addition, she was elected in 2022 to the Program Committee of the [[American Chemical Society|ACS Division of Biological Chemistry]], contributing to the planning of national symposia.
